lesson.title: Undoing in the right order

lead.text: Take a round of the number game with two jobs in it. “I'm thinking of a number. I treble it and then take away 9. I get 21.” The last job was taking away 9, so that comes off first: 21 plus 9 is 30. The job before it was trebling, so that comes off next: 30 divided by 3 is 10.

afterFigure.text: The picture runs the round forwards. Treble 10 to get 30, then take away 9 to get 21. The order you undo in matters. If you undo the jobs in the order they were done, dividing by 3 first and then adding 9, you reach 16. Treble 16 and take away 9 and you get 39, which isn't 21.

It is the same idea as the shoes and socks. Whatever was done last has to be undone first, and each job is undone by its opposite. Read from the result back to the start, a calculation gives you the number you began with. That is what solving an equation with several moves comes to.

lead.text: Two jobs this time. Start from the result and take the jobs off, last job first.

reveal.text: You took off the 4 first, then undid the doubling. The next screen shows how to read the order of the jobs from an equation.

steps.headline: Reading the jobs from an equation

lead.text: An equation records its jobs in shorthand. Take 2x + 5 = 11. You met the rule for reading 2x + 5 in the first lesson: multiplication comes before addition. So the left side says: start with x, double it, then add 5. The result of those jobs is 11.

afterFigure.text: Run it backwards from 11. The last job was adding 5, so take 5 away to get 6. The job before it was doubling, so halve the 6 to get 3. The machine in the picture agrees: put in 3 and 11 comes out.

On the scales those two backward steps are the two moves from the last lesson. Subtract 5 from both sides, then divide both sides by 2. The moves come in the reverse of the order of the jobs, so reading the left side tells you where to begin. The next example writes the moves out as equations.

lead.text: Read the jobs first: 5x − 3 means multiply by 5, then take away 3. The last job is taking away 3, so that comes off first.

workedSteps.text: The last job was − 3, so add 3 to both sides first.
Then undo the × 5: divide both sides by 5.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Read the jobs on x, take the last one off first, then carry on. The first line is a question about the route, and the lines after it write the route out.

workedSteps.text: Read the jobs on x in 2x + 3, then choose the route that undoes them.
Subtract 3 from both sides. It undoes the last job.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Name the last job first. Then undo it on both sides, and undo the job before.

reveal.text: You undid the jobs in the opposite order to the one the expression was built in.

lead.text: In every equation so far the last job was easy to spot. Brackets can hide it. They are the curved marks around part of an expression, as in 3(x + 2), and they tell you to work out what is inside first and treat the result as one package. A number written next to a bracket means multiply, just as 3x does. So in 3(x + 2) the 2 is added to x first. The whole package is then multiplied by 3.

afterFigure.text: The jobs run in the order add 2, then multiply by 3, so multiplying by 3 is the last job. That makes it the first to undo: divide both sides by 3, which opens the package. Then take away the 2. Compare 3x + 2, where the 2 sits outside the multiplication and is added last. Brackets change which job comes last.
The same method works for any number of layers. List the jobs in the order the expression builds them, starting inside the brackets. Then take them off from the other end.

lead.text: Find the last job in 3(x + 2), take it off first, then deal with what is inside the package.

reveal.text: The 3 multiplies the whole package, so it comes off first. Then the + 2 comes off.

steps.headline: Answers that are not whole numbers

lead.text: In the first lesson you tested 3 in 5x − 2 = 12 and the left side came to 13, one too many. No whole number fits, but you can find the solution now. The last job in 5x − 2 is taking away 2, so add 2 to both sides to get 5x = 14. Then divide both sides by 5.

afterFigure.text: Fourteen divided by 5 does not come out even. It is the fraction 14/5, or 2.8 as a decimal. Check by running the machine forwards: 5 × 2.8 is 14, and 14 − 2 is 12. Slide the input in the picture to 2.8 and the target is met.

Nothing in the method asks for a whole-number answer. When the last division leaves a remainder, write the answer as a fraction or a decimal. A fraction such as 14/5 is exact, and a decimal is sometimes a rounded copy of it.

lead.text: Division is a job like any other. Write x ÷ 4 for x shared into four equal parts, and multiplying by 4 undoes it. Undo each job with its opposite, last job first.

lesson.orientation: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.
lesson.nextAction: Place a point from its coordinates and read coordinates back off a plotted point.

blocks.text: You put your socks on before your shoes. Getting undressed runs the other way: the shoes come off first, then the socks. Do it the wrong way round and the socks end up outside the shoes. Nobody has to think about it, because the order of the first job decides the order of the second.

Calculations work like that. An expression such as 2x + 3 is a short list of jobs done to a number: here, double it and then add 3. To find the number you started with, you take the jobs off again, and the order matters as much as it does with shoes.

The last lesson had equations with two moves, and the examples told you which move to make first. This lesson explains why that order works, so you can choose it yourself. It also covers an expression such as 3(x + 2), where the order is less obvious.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo a calculation one step at a time, last step first, to find the number you started with.

recap.keyIdea: To find x, undo the operations in reverse order, last one first, doing the same to both sides each time.

blocks.text: You solved 5x − 3 = 12 by adding 3 and then dividing by 5, and in 3(x + 2) = 21 you divided by the outside 3 before taking off the 2. You also found that 5x − 2 = 12 gives x = 2.8, which trying whole numbers could never have reached.

recap.nextHook: Next the numbers go onto a grid, where a pair of them pins down a single point.

questions.prompt: I think of a number, double it, then add 4. I get 20. What is my number?
hints: Start from the answer and work backwards.
The last thing I did was add 4. Take it off first.
Now undo the doubling: what number doubles to give what is left?
questions.onCorrect: 8. You undid the steps backwards, last step first. That is the habit this lesson builds.

misconceptions.feedback: You added 4. The last step was adding 4, so take it off.
That undoes the + 4 but not the doubling. One more step back.

questions.prompt: Which route undoes “multiply by 2, then add 3”?
hints: Undo the last operation in the forward route first.
Use the inverse of addition, then the inverse of multiplication.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Undo the last operation first: subtract 3, then divide by 2. Applying inverses in the forward order would change the calculation.

questions.onCorrect: Subtract 3, then divide by 2. The last step comes off first, using its inverse.

misconceptions.feedback: That undoes the steps in the order they were done. The last step has to come off first.
The numbers are swapped. The 3 was added, so 3 is what comes off; the 2 was the multiplier.

hints: The addition of 3 happens after multiplication by 2.
Subtract 3 from both sides to leave 2x = 14.
Divide by 2, then check by multiplying and adding in the original order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 3 gives 2x = 14; dividing by 2 gives x = 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Subtracting 3 and then dividing by 2 undoes the machine in reverse order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 2x. One more step: undo the × 2.
You added 3. The + 3 is undone by subtracting 3.
You divided before taking off the 3. The last step has to come off first.

hints: Here multiplication by 3 surrounds the whole bracket.
Divide both sides by 3 before changing x + 2.
Then undo the remaining addition of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dividing by 3 gives x + 2 = 7; subtracting 2 gives x = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The 3 multiplies the whole package, so divide by 3 first, then take off the 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x + 2. The package is still closed: take off the 2 too.
You subtracted 2 first. The 3 multiplies the whole bracket, so it comes off first.

hints: The final operation is subtracting 2.
Add 2 to both sides to leave x / 4 = 3.5.
Undo division by 4 with multiplication by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adding 2 gives x / 4 = 3.5; multiplying by 4 gives x = 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Add 2 to both sides, then multiply both sides by 4 to undo the division.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x ÷ 4. Undo the division as well, by multiplying.
You multiplied but skipped the + 2. The subtraction is the last step, so it comes off first.

hints: Undo the final subtraction before undoing multiplication.
Add 4 to both sides of 3x − 4 = 14.
Divide the resulting right-hand side by 3.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Add 4 to both sides to undo the − 4, then divide both sides by 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 3x. Divide both sides by 3 to leave x alone.
That is 14 − 4. The − 4 is undone by adding 4.

choices.label: The − 3 was the last step, so it comes off first.

acceptedIdeas: The − 3 was the last step, so it comes off first.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The − 3 was the last step, so it comes off first.

questions.onCorrect: Undo in the reverse order: the last step in the expression is the first one off.

misconceptions.feedback: No rule puts adding first. It depends on which step was done last in the expression.
The order matters. Divide first and the − 3 would be divided too.

hints: Replace x with 7. What is 2 × 7?
Now add the 3.
Multiply first, then add.
questions.onCorrect: 17, the right side of the equation. Running the machine forward checks the answer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 × 7. The expression then adds 3.
2x means 2 × x, so it is 2 × 7, not 2 + 7.

hints: Work backwards through the outside operations.
Remove the outside addition, then divide by the multiplier outside the bracket.
The expression is now x − 1; undo that last subtraction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract 2, divide by 4, then add 1: x = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Take off the + 2, divide by the outside 4, then add 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x − 1. Undo the subtraction inside the brackets as well.
That is what the whole bracketed part is worth. The outside multiplier and the brackets still have to come off.

questions.prompt: Solve 4x + 1 = 4. You may enter a fraction.
hints: First remove the +1 term on both sides.
This leaves 4x = 3.
Division can give a fraction; x need not be a whole number.
questions.onCorrect: 0.75, or 3 ÷ 4. Subtract 1, then divide by 4. An answer need not be whole.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of 4x. Divide both sides by 4 to leave x alone.
You added 1. The + 1 is undone by subtracting 1.

hints: Undo the outside addition of 1 first.
After subtracting 1, x / 2 must equal 3.
Multiply both sides by 2, then substitute your answer back.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtracting 1 gives x / 2 = 3; doubling gives x = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Subtract 1, then multiply both sides by 2 to undo the division.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value of x ÷ 2. Undo the division as well.
You added 1. The + 1 is undone by subtracting 1.

questions.prompt: In 5(x − 2), which is the last step?
questions.onCorrect: The × 5 is last: it multiplies the whole package, so it comes off first.

misconceptions.feedback: The subtraction happens inside the brackets, which are worked out first.
You can. Brackets are worked out first, so what is outside them comes last.
